title: Papers & Boards: Sources, Types & Properties
description: From wood pulp to finished sheet: sources, common types and working properties of paper and board.
content_html:
Where Paper and Board Come From

Paper and board begin as wood pulp — a slurry of cellulose fibres extracted from softwood trees such as pine and spruce. Timber is chipped, then either mechanically ground or chemically treated (the kraft process) to break the wood into individual fibres. Chemical pulping removes more lignin, producing a stronger, more durable sheet; mechanical pulping is cheaper but results in a weaker, more acidic paper that yellows over time. Alongside virgin wood pulp, the industry relies heavily on recycled fibre recovered from used newspapers, cardboard boxes and office paper. Recycled content reduces demand on forests and the energy needed to process raw timber.

Sustainable sourcing is increasingly important. The FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) certifies paper products whose raw materials come from forests managed to strict environmental, social and economic standards. FSC-certified paper guarantees that for every tree felled, replanting or natural regeneration takes place. Designers specifying paper for a product brief should always consider whether FSC certification is required by the client or demanded by the target market.

How Paper and Board Are Made

Pulp is mixed with large quantities of water to form a dilute slurry containing roughly 99% water. This slurry is sprayed onto a moving wire mesh (the Fourdrinier machine), where water drains through the mesh and the fibres begin to mat together. The wet web of fibres then passes through a series of press rollers that squeeze out more water, followed by heated drying cylinders that evaporate the remainder. The result is a continuous roll of paper. To make board, multiple plies of pulp are layered and pressed together while still wet, increasing thickness and rigidity. Coating with clay or chalk and calendering (pressing between smooth rollers) creates a smooth, printable surface.

Key Fact

Paper is measured in grams per square metre (GSM or g/m²). Below 170 g/m² is generally classed as paper; above 170 g/m² is classed as card or board. Typical photocopier paper is 80 g/m²; a cereal-box folding boxboard is around 280–350 g/m².

Common Papers and Their Uses

The paper family includes a wide range of specialist sheets, each engineered for a specific design or production purpose:

  • Cartridge paper — a thick, slightly textured paper (90–135 g/m²) used for hand drawing, sketching and painting. Its surface tooth holds pencil, ink and watercolour well.
  • Layout paper — lightweight and semi-transparent, allowing designers to trace and overlay ideas quickly during the initial design stages.
  • Tracing paper — highly transparent, used to copy drawings precisely or to create overlays that show different layers of a design separately.
  • Grid paper — pre-printed with squares, isometric dots or perspective grids to assist accurate technical drawing without specialist equipment.
  • Bleed-proof paper — specially coated so marker pen ink does not spread beyond the drawn line, giving sharp, clean edges in rendered design visuals.
  • Sugar paper — a rough, recycled-content paper available in a wide colour range, used for mounting, display work and craft activities.

Common Boards and Their Properties

Boards are stiffer, thicker and more rigid than papers. Each type is engineered for specific structural or commercial applications:

  • Corrugated card — a sandwich structure with a fluted (wavy) inner layer between two flat liner sheets. The flutes act as columns, giving excellent compressive strength and cushioning, ideal for transit packaging and product boxes.
  • Duplex board — a board with a bleached white top layer for printing and a grey recycled-fibre back. Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost. Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost.
  • Solid white board (SWB) — made entirely from virgin bleached chemical pulp, giving a brilliant white surface on both sides. Higher-grade and more expensive than duplex board; used for premium packaging where colour accuracy is critical.
  • Foil-lined board — a paper or board laminated to a thin aluminium foil layer on one side, providing a moisture and gas barrier. Used in food packaging (butter wrappers, confectionery cartons, coffee pouches) and drinks cartons.
  • Foam board — a polystyrene foam core sandwiched between two sheets of smooth paper. Extremely lightweight yet rigid; used for architectural models, point-of-sale displays and exhibition graphics.
  • Inkjet card — a smooth, coated card optimised for home or office inkjet printing, giving sharp colour reproduction. Common weight: 160–300 g/m².
  • Mount board — a thick, acid-free board (approximately 1,400 microns) available in many colours, used to frame and display artwork or photographs without yellowing over time.

Paper weight in GSM (grams per square metre) measures mass, not physical thickness — a dense coated paper can be heavier in GSM yet thinner than a bulkier uncoated sheet of the same GSM. For board, physical thickness is often quoted in microns (micrometres, µm) — one micron is one thousandth of a millimetre. A standard cereal box folding boxboard is around 280–350 g/m² and approximately 400–500 microns thick. When a designer specifies board for a packaging brief, both figures may be relevant: GSM determines postage cost and stiffness calculations, while micron thickness determines whether the net will fit together at scored folds.

Callipers measure board thickness in microns. A micrometer screw gauge gives precise readings to 1–2 microns. In a workshop, a simple rule of thumb is that 1 micron ≈ 1 g/m² for uncoated boards, but this ratio shifts once clay coating is applied.

Physical and Working Properties

When selecting a paper or board, designers must consider several key properties. Stiffness (resistance to bending) increases with thickness and with the grain direction of the fibres — paper is considerably stiffer when bent against the grain. Porosity affects ink absorption; coated boards absorb less ink, giving sharper printed images. Opacity describes how much light passes through; a high-opacity sheet prevents text from showing through to the reverse side. Whiteness influences perceived print quality; a brighter white base improves colour vibrancy. Tear resistance is highest parallel to the grain direction. Tensile strength measures resistance to being pulled apart; kraft paper, used for paper bags and envelopes, has high tensile strength due to long chemical pulp fibres.

Key Fact

Paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction) during manufacture. Paper and board fold more cleanly, crease more crisply and are stiffer along the grain. When cutting nets for packaging, the grain direction should run parallel to the longest fold lines to prevent cracking and produce a neater carton.

Ecological and Social Footprint

Paper production has significant environmental impacts. Pulp mills consume large quantities of water (up to 10 litres per sheet of A4) and energy, and the chemical bleaching process produces chlorine-based by-products if elemental chlorine is used. Modern mills increasingly use totally chlorine-free (TCF) or elemental chlorine-free (ECF) bleaching to reduce toxic effluent. Deforestation is a key concern: illegal logging for paper pulp destroys biodiversity and releases stored carbon. FSC certification and recycled-content labelling allow consumers and designers to make informed choices. Socially, paper mills in developing countries have faced criticism for poor working conditions and displacement of indigenous forest communities — ethical procurement policies address this by requiring supplier audits.

Recycled fibre uses significantly less water and energy than virgin pulp, and diverts waste from landfill. Each time a fibre is recycled, however, it shortens slightly, reducing the strength and quality of the resulting sheet. Recycled board typically has a grey or brown appearance, which is why duplex board uses a white virgin-pulp surface layer over a recycled grey back. High-quality printing generally requires a proportion of virgin fibre to maintain brightness and smoothness.

The ideal solution for most packaging applications is a mixed-content board: recycled fibre for the structural core layers where strength per unit weight matters less, and virgin or de-inked pulp for the outer printing surface. This approach balances environmental performance against the technical requirements of modern printing and surface finishing.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to name or describe a paper or board, always include three elements: the name of the material, a key property (e.g. lightweight, stiff, transparent), and a specific use (e.g. cereal packaging, architectural models). Answers that name only the material without linking it to a property and purpose rarely score full marks on 3-mark or 4-mark questions. For sustainability questions, go beyond simply writing ‘it is recycled’ — state what that means in practice (reduced water use, shorter fibres, lower energy demand).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Paper and board are made from wood pulp or recycled fibre; FSC certification guarantees responsible forest management. Weight is measured in GSM and thickness in microns, and the two do not always correspond directly.
  • Common papers (cartridge, layout, tracing, bleed-proof, sugar) are selected for specific design and drawing tasks; common boards (corrugated, duplex, solid white, foil-lined, foam, mount) are chosen for packaging, modelling and display based on their structural and surface properties.
  • Fibre grain direction, stiffness, opacity, porosity and tensile strength are critical working properties. Recycled-content boards reduce environmental impact but sacrifice some printability; mixed-content boards balance both.

glossary_terms.definition: Cellulose fibres separated from wood or recycled paper to make new paper or board products.
An international organisation that certifies timber and paper products sourced from responsibly managed forests.
Board made from a fluted inner layer sandwiched between two flat liner sheets, giving excellent strength-to-weight ratio.
The direction in which paper fibres align during manufacture; paper is stiffer and tears more cleanly parallel to this direction.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of board is made from a fluted inner layer sandwiched between two flat liner sheets?
A) Solid white board
B) Duplex board
C) Corrugated card
D) Mount board
Name two papers suitable for use in the initial design development stages of a graphics project.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: layout paper / tracing paper / cartridge paper / bleed-proof paper / grid paper. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper is manufactured from wood pulp.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- Wood is chipped and treated to separate cellulose fibres into a pulp slurry.
- The slurry is spread onto a moving wire mesh where water drains away and fibres mat together.
- The web passes through press rollers and heated drying cylinders to remove remaining moisture and form a continuous roll. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why grain direction is important when cutting and folding a net for a cardboard carton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- During manufacture, paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction).
- Paper and board are considerably stiffer when bent against the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.
- Folding against the grain can crack the surface coating and weaken the structure of the carton.
- Specifying grain direction correctly during print finishing reduces waste and improves the quality of the assembled box. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging designer might choose duplex board rather than solid white board for a breakfast cereal box, considering both performance and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Duplex board has a white bleached top surface suitable for high-quality printing, meeting the visual requirements of cereal-box branding.
- The grey recycled-fibre back layer reduces raw material cost compared with solid white board, which uses 100% virgin chemical pulp.
- Using recycled fibre in the core layers reduces energy consumption and water use during manufacture, lowering the carbon footprint of the packaging.
- Solid white board offers superior whiteness and colour accuracy, which may be justified for premium products where brand colour precision is critical.
- For a budget cereal brand, the cost saving of duplex board outweighs the marginal loss in print quality; for a luxury brand, solid white board may be justified.
[6 marks - Mastering: Balanced comparison referencing both material performance and sustainability with application to the cereal box context. Secure: Performance and sustainability points made but comparison lacks full development. Developing: One board described well; limited comparison. Emerging: Basic identification only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using recycled fibre rather than virgin wood pulp in the manufacture of paper and board products.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
- Recycled fibre uses significantly less energy and water than processing virgin wood pulp, reducing the environmental impact of manufacture.
- Using recycled content diverts waste paper and board from landfill, extending the useful life of the raw material.
- Recycled-content products can carry on-pack environmental claims that appeal to environmentally conscious consumers and retail buyers.
- Reduces demand for virgin timber, helping to protect forests and the biodiversity they support.
Disadvantages:
- Each recycling cycle shortens the cellulose fibres, reducing tensile strength and making it harder to produce high-quality printing surfaces.
- Recycled board is typically grey or brown in colour; achieving a white surface requires a virgin-fibre top ply, adding cost and complexity.
- Ink contamination in recycled streams must be removed by de-inking, which adds a processing stage and produces sludge waste requiring disposal.
- The quality and availability of recycled fibre fluctuates with consumer recycling rates, making supply chains less predictable than virgin pulp sourcing.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to real design or manufacturing contexts. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance between sides. Emerging: One-sided response or very superficial points.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes paper or board whose raw material comes from responsibly managed forests?
At approximately what GSM does a material transition from paper to card or board?
Bleed-proof paper is specially coated so that _____ ink does not spread beyond the drawn line.
Paper is stiffer and folds more cleanly when bent _____ the grain direction.
Match each board type to its key characteristic:
right: Fluted inner layer gives compressive strength
Polystyrene core makes it lightweight and rigid
Acid-free; used to display artwork without yellowing

flashcard_questions.a: Cellulose fibres separated from wood or recycled paper, used to make paper and board.

flashcard_questions.q: What does FSC certification guarantee about a paper product?
flashcard_questions.a: Its raw materials come from responsibly managed forests where replanting takes place.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the unit used to measure paper weight?
flashcard_questions.a: Grams per square metre (GSM or g/m²).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the unit used to measure board thickness?
flashcard_questions.a: Microns (micrometres, µm); one micron is one thousandth of a millimetre.

flashcard_questions.q: Which paper type has a semi-transparent quality for tracing and overlaying designs?
flashcard_questions.a: Layout paper is semi-transparent; tracing paper is fully transparent.

flashcard_questions.q: What structural feature gives corrugated card its compressive strength?
flashcard_questions.a: A fluted (wavy) inner layer sandwiched between two flat liner sheets.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is duplex board used for most food cartons rather than solid white board?
flashcard_questions.a: It has a white printable surface but uses a cheaper recycled-fibre grey back layer.

flashcard_questions.q: Which board type is best for architectural models due to its light weight?
flashcard_questions.a: Foam board, which has a polystyrene core between two paper facing sheets.

flashcard_questions.q: What does porosity affect in a paper or board?
flashcard_questions.a: How much ink is absorbed; lower porosity gives sharper printed images.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the machine direction in paper manufacture?
flashcard_questions.a: The direction fibres align during production; paper is stiffer and tears more cleanly along it.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one environmental benefit of using recycled fibre in paper production.
flashcard_questions.a: It uses less energy and water than virgin pulp and diverts waste from landfill.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does paper weaken with each recycling cycle?
flashcard_questions.a: Cellulose fibres shorten each time they are processed, reducing strength.
